Stellaris is one of those games that actually was great, and continued to get great updates. I personally stopped at Niven (2.1) for a LONG time, as I wasn't a fan of 2.2. Just recently, some friends and I figured "what the heck", and took the plunge into 2.7.

It was a mistake.

The game added so much amazing material (lithoids, federations, more superstructures). We even adjusted to the EARLY GAME (emphasis explained soon) planetary UI. It was not as simple, but we figured there would be ways to do something about that later. When we got to the midgame, however, things started to unravel. AI sporting multi 100k fleets 100 years in, 200k awakened empire fleets beating the tar out of similarly sized PC fleets (who had contender, might I add), things got wonky. And when the fun stuff started clearly playing to the advantage of the AI, the real underlying issue of stellaris was laid bare for us all to see.

The micro is killing any and all enjoyment.

Planets now need to balance workers, jobs, amenities, food, energy, minerals, alloys, and housing. On each planet. Every single one. Don't want to micro? Ohhh boy, here's the bad news. If you neglect jobs or housing, the pops on your planet will get upset. When they get upset, you lose productivity. When you lose productivity, you go negative in just about every resource. When you go negative, you can't colonize new planets, build new habitats (artificial planets for the uninitiated), and you spiral into literally pausing the game every month to see what you can afford to fix. 

The irony? The game has an "automate" switch you can flick to ignore this and hope the AI for your empire can balance things. They'll also dip in the red, but tend to stay above water as long as you are constantly expanding. If you stop though, you die. But this raises the question; If you could automate the system, if it was such a requested feature that it made it through testing and into the game...why would that system even be implemented?

Yes, I'm biased, I'll take full responsibility for that. 2.1 had a perfectly functioning system of pop management. The rest of the game's wonky issues with AI power scaling could maybe, MAYBE be worked around by having all the PCs work together and stand as one under the awesome new fed system, but the pop management is literally so bad, I cannot even approach it any longer. That was AFTER spending 40+ hours trying my best to tame it.

So, why is this still a recommendation? 

Well, for one, it's a fantastic game that some people more invested in the microing would greatly enjoy. I'd personally say there's no better space based 4x out there. That and, there's a magic button to restore my games to 2.1 Niven.

In regards to the 2.0 changes I'll not be addressing the flavor of starting weapons as it makes no sense to have an empire ignore all other possibilities of potential in armaments. An example why this is less flavor and more a design flaw is that we humans have already conquered two of these. So to imply a certain empire only has rockets on their spaceships makes no sense.

[Example: Combat Jets already use kinetics and explosives.] 
[u]There for as of release of 2.0 all the empires start with all the starting weapon techs.[/u]

Another thing a lot of people seem to have been complaining about is the removal of warp and wormhole FTL travel because hyperdrive was made the default choice. Anyone who has played a hyperdrive only game before 2.0 will know it results in a more strategic experience.  Pre 2.0 these FTL types were a total mess.  Wormhole travel was overpowered. Warp incredibly slow and hyperdrives incredibly fast. 

You had empires which use wormhole travel be capable of popping up anywhere in your space, meaning they could land on your capital with their entire fleet. Whereas a weaker hyperdrive FTL empire could just infinitely outrun you and you'd have no hope of catching them while they terrorize you and your stations. The release of 2.0 decided balancing all of this was impossible because of how different they are. Indeed, nerfing all the FTL types would simply declare all of them eventually as useless or in the end there'd be one FTL type that is better than the others (as was previously the case due to PDX attempting to balance the FTL types through a number of patches). 

[b]There for as of release of 2.0: The default FTL type is THE HYPERDRIVE which follows hyperdrive lanes generated by the map. Paradox effectively leveled the playing field with these changes and fixed some of the innate problems related to traversing the galactic landscape.[/b]

[u]Better yet wormholes were not entirely removed; they were crafted into intergalactic phenomena that can be explored and lead from one side of the galaxy to another. In fact these wormholes have certain events and anomalies attached to them, making the exploration of wormholes a tad bit more exciting. [/u] Clearly controlling a wormhole is now a matter of strategic importance. It can lead you to unexplored space if you are boxed in and it can serve as the perfect choice for "flanking" the enemy in case of heavy defense installations.

The possibilities clearly ended up in the favor of the game instead of having entirely removed wormholes. As a result, anyone can go through the wormholes. Depending on your luck, these wormholes can be your demise or your key to success. In addition - empires can now create or repair Gateways that can lead to any allied point in space. Meaning enemies can’t abuse it like the wormholes and you and your allies can have strategically placed Gateways between your capitals.

Indeed, Stellaris felt and played as a new game. A lot of people played this game in this semi broken state that WORKED but was far from perfect.  It tricked the present players who eventually fell out of sight on how things SHOULD be. Paradox clearly hadn't intended this game to carry on as a half-baked, ill planned product. There for when 2.0 arrived it did so in style. It conquered previously well-established exploits that players used to cheese the game.

It was the case your borders grew exponentially. You could research to improve this growth and how you came to control systems depended on this sphere of influence. This hardly made sense as it often put you in control over systems you had no interest in or would realistically have no influence over. The borders were often a garbled mess. It meant you had no control over what you owned. PDX finally decided to redo this and introduce starbases, removing the exponentially growing borders altogether. Each system now needs a starbase constructed there in order to be owned and in return PDX introduced a claim system to claim these areas. The game evolved from being all about planets to being all about systems. It could just be the case you’re staring down at an enemy you do not want a planet of, before Apocalypse you were forced to take these planets. Now you are not. This enabled players to strategize about what part of space they wanted to be theirs. Giving them direct control over what they own and who they border with. 

Another critical change to Stellaris was the introduction of Fleet Command points. The idea that all fleets had to be doomstacks in order for you to win not only lagged the game but removed the concept of multiple fleets in multiple locations defending from potentially different threats. Not only that but pre 2.0 there was no way to play defensively. With the introduction of starbases this has changed. You can now effectively have a secured border with defense installations that can rack up to 40k firepower. You won’t see the AI hurrying to get through that and quite frankly on higher difficulty I’ve been stopped by such defenses more than once. Whereas before, trying to play defensively was a good joke. Any decent fleet worth its salt would just fly through the system as if all the minerals you spent on fortifying said system did not exist. The key issues to not having a defense and making the game revolve around said doomstacks is the fact once your fleet was gone you were free to reload. Splitting up fleets and making defensive installations possible prevents all that. There for adding to the depth of warfare in Stellaris. This is without even mentioning the under the hood changes to spaceships themselves. Some players might come to miss the big battles between fleets, doomstack vs doomstack. Though really it was only a matter of “I’m gonna zerg rush you better than you are going to zerg rush me”. 

[b]So really, if I haven’t convinced you that PDX has the best intentions for this game then I don’t know what will. In the end, Stellaris is a great game and PDX is a great company. The changes made were changes necessary. You won’t see me running back to 1.9. There’s nothing better about it and as time goes on 1.9 will be so out of date that the purpose of even staying with that patch will be brought to question by those who even try to cling to it as if it’s going to change something.[/b]

Updated Review:

I've recently tried to give the game another go now that it's been a couple years or so since the "Custodian Team" has been formed to deal with long-standing issues. There are a few improvements I've noticed, but ultimately and unfortunately my old review still stands up, especially for new players.

Performance has been improved noticeably in the early game, which is the reason they sliced all of the population numbers in half so at least I'm glad to see it was for a good reason. However the performance still suffers terribly as the game progresses. Graphics look much nicer, lots of new environmental effects and pretty lights to look at. The game does appear quite pretty now, though it tends to chug a bit if you get too close especially with big ship battles (this is an older issue that doesn't seem to have a fix.) The AI also seems to be less brain-dead, but I still see them making really confusing decisions like endlessly expanding into objectively terrible systems and overbuilding habitats.

I've noticed some new problems too, like how the AI seems way too eager to become a vassal of another empire instead of forming pacts or federations. I also have noticed there are hardly any wars at all anymore. I was playing as a auth/fan materialist technocracy and somehow I've ended up with 5 out of the nine major empires as my subjects, I've only fought one war in 150 years, and it was the ONLY war to happen in the entire galaxy. Even fanatic militarists aren't going to war at all.

Unfortunately as I mentioned previously, there hasn't been enough of an improvement to change my overall review, especially in the context of a new player to the game:

- DLCs are still insanely expensive, especially if you have to start from scratch.
- Species packs are overpriced for something that you could find on the workshop for free (ie: new portraits, trait and civic expansion packs.)
- New DLC launches are __STILL__ being released in a game-breaking state, this includes the free updates that get rolled out to players that did NOT buy the DLC. I have no idea how they can __STILL__ screw this up after all of these years. Absolutely mind-boggling!

I did not buy either of the two latest "feature" DLCs (Nemesis, Overlord) because they have very mixed reviews, again suffering from old, core design issues that I've discussed/ranted about in my original review: adding new half-baked features instead of expanding old ones, or adding new unbalanced options to existing features (eg: new Overlord subject types being either overpowered or garbage trap picks, same with new megastructures.)

The game still has life, but in my opinion is for the majority thanks to the hard, unpaid labour from the members of the incredibly robust modding community.

Honest truth is, this game gave me the best feeling of being a small being in a grand universe, always feeling like the next corner of space we rounded would show us some unexpected wonder about the nature of things. This is the best existentialism game I've played except for maybe the Talos Principle, and this may be the best depiction of our lonely place in the great expanse that I've ever seen. But I cannot recommend it, as it stands.

What the game absolutely nails in its atmosphere, lore, and wonder, it largely betrays with the simple shell of a RTS model it chooses to employ. Did we not learn our lessons about doomstacks from Civilization IV? For the countless ways that this is the true spiritual successor to Civilization on a grander, space scale (talking to you, Beyond Earth), it's amazing they succumb to these simple flaws in designing a game that is, at the basic level, fun.

The management of your resources, colonies, research, and policies is spot-on, but just like in any multiplayer RTS, all serve as secondary (albeit important and highly necessary) elements to the combat. Most of the intricate and exciting early game land grabs and stage-setting for galactic domination ends up boiling down to a very limited number, or even just one, single space battle where the entirety of one civilization's fleet squares off against the enemy's. The tiny nuanced advantages in balanced fleet compositions (excluding if someone is WAY behind on research, of course) become irrelevant behind "the big number" of fleet power, and once one side starts losing, the snowball just continues into an utter stomp. You cannot control any individual tactics, no formations, it's basically just however the AI decides to use weaponry you've customized, and there rarely appears to be any viable strategy beyond piling every ship you own into a ball and either chasing their ball of ships across the galaxy (if you have a better combat number) or running while you try to amass a bigger ball (if you have a worse combat number).

The rudimentary nature almost akin to a cell phone game just feels so out of place in an otherwise nearly perfect game. It sinks the unique experience into a monotony in almost every match while you wade through the mid- to late-game. Until something is adjusted on these lines, I'm going to have to regrettably recommend against this game.

Having played over 1500 hours of Stellaris I can confidently say that it's a brilliant game. From the concept to the myriad of gameplay features, story elements and the beautiful visuals. As a grand strategy game, I see this as Paradox's best.

For the past couple of years however, the studio's bad practices have gotten worse. Unfortunately most game developers and publishers are severely lacking in the "listening to the playerbase" department, so that's nothing new. But it seems Paradox has joined the more elite club of telling the playerbase what they should be concerned about.

The developers are and have been aware of the many, many issues in the game for years. For the longest time the community was worried about the ungodly endgame lag. And more recently the main gripes have been with update 3.8 and it's unnecessary revisions to game mechanics that the playerbase was largely quite happy with. A large number of issues were reported to PDX when the update was launched and many of the smaller problems were fixed relatively soon.

Which brings us to today, with a new dlc having been published a few days ago. We have had half a year of contending with the massive, game breaking bugs and lag that the previous updates brought, a new system for leaders in the game that nobody wanted and crippling issues that have become a "natural" part of the game, some dating back to it's launch.

Paradox is aware of all these problems with their product, and they have had years to iron out these problems. Instead we get new dlcs (as always) and silence on the studio's part, whenever players converse on the forums about these massive shortcomings. Anyone who has played this game for a long time knows better than to expect concrete, dedicated solutions to their concerns, but there are many people who still buy this game today, hoping to delve into a cool 4x, grand strategy campaign.

So, to those who are thinking about buying this game, the price is not unreasonable, it is high, but you can get it for cheaper during sales which happen quite often. The money is worth it for the base game. For the DLCs, it is not. You will end up spending 200+ €/$ as a very conservative estimate in order to get all the content the game is intended to be played with. And if you fall in love with this game, you will get to play it always keeping in mind that the studio and publisher that made it, does not care if the product is broken. Or if the community that has sank so much money into playing their game are all crying out for solutions to obvious, game breaking problems. So the game is good, the business model reprehensible and the studio uncaring. Choice is yours.

[h1]500 hours [/h1]
I just saw that I have over 500 hours put into this game and I think it might be a good moment to review this game, especially after the 2.0 update which changed the game so fundamentally, it's like a new game.

[b]What is this game about?[/b]
You create a Civilization that just had made its breakthrough to achieve Faster Than Light (FTL) travel and is about to leave it's own solar system for the first time.

Expect Grand Strategy decisions. This is about the progress of your Civilization, less a question of what one single Spaceship does (although you can order Ships around!). You Explore and Colonize the galaxy until you start meeting other Civilizations that might be more, less or equally advanced and you decide if you will try to be their friends or their enemies. The game has no real goal. You can win by exterminating all other Civilizations or by conquering 40% of the galaxy (or 60% if you form a federation).

You can construct buildings on planets to improve your resource output and you can construct structues in space, mostly to get resources as well so this game is much about economy and less about tactical decisions.

You can research new technologies and Ideas that will give you new or better stuff to build. You can construct fleets and control them but don't expect careful fleet management decisions from this game. This is not a game about Fleet Formations but about politics, economy with a roleplaying flavour.

Wait, roleplay?
Yes! Since you have total control over the design process of your species you can just play the style you want. About anything you have seen in SciFi is represented in this game. It can be ridicusly funny to create a species of flesh eating butterflies or cute looking orchids trying to exterminate everyone else.
You know a particular SciFi trope you love? It is mos likely included in this game.

Can I...?
Yes, you CAN construct a Dyson Sphere, you CAN Terraform planets, alter a species genes, transform your Civilization into immortal machines or Spell wielding Psions! There IS a terminator like Rise of the machines event and things can go horribly, horribly wrong. I mean.. fall of the Eldar level wrong!
And yes, since the latest expansion you CAN build a Death Star!

[b]The bad[/b]
Not every style of play is supported equally. Especially if you try to play in a peaceful way, you will encounter some walls. Diplomacy has its limitations. Don't expect to go all StarFleet and turn your enemies into Federation Members (although it is possible). 

[b] Well, who is this game for? [/b]
This game is for people that like the idea of taking control of a full civilization and shape it. Expect Civilization level of control. This game is falling on the odd side of Paradox Grand Strategy games. It doesn't give you the complexity of Europa Universalis (although this might be a big plus if you feel overwhelmed by EU) and it doesn't offer 1/10 of the detail Crusader Kings. In my opinion, Stellaris is more like the "entry point to paradox games" as it includes many very intuitive mechanics you can encounter in other strategy games while also giving a hint of the complex systems you can encounter in the more "hardcore" paradox Strategy games. 

It is also a game for people that love Space SciFi and can't get enough of Star Trek (really, this game contains so many Star Trek tropes!).

I don't know... I wish there was a "Maybe" recommendation. See, when you first start playing this game, you will be overwhelmed with all kinds of amazing variety of cultural and lifestyle choices for your species like government, traditions to be a pacifist who focuses on expanding, or a warmonger who wants to assert dominance on other species, or devouring swarms/fanatic purifiers who just want to destroy all life. Focus on science, I even had a science species transcend their mortal flesh and literally all convert to a species of AI/robots it was pretty cool.

I can't say this game sucks. I can't say "I don't recommend it". I got 100+ hours in it and I enjoyed those hours.

What I can say is don't believe that, in the current state of the game, it is a sandbox game. The game starts off with you trying to develop and enjoy your species' culture and traditions and roleplay them out a bit, but every single time you hit mid game and then worse in late game, it is ONLY about war and military.

You will find no where to expand without having to conquor thy neighbor. The victory conditions require war, even the federation victory requires war if you need to force other species to adopt your government and traditional styles. 

You can avoid war if you are a very diplomatic and loveable species to a greater degree, but there's nothing to do BUT war in mid-late game for the most part. Research is all done and you're just researching the infinitely progressing stuff like add +1 to core sector system or 10% HP to army health etc.

You can go megastructures but let's be realistic, why? By the time you're in a position where you can both get them and afford to build them, the only one that actually benefits is the habitat and maybe a dyson sphere if you want to go over your naval capacity you can amass a ton of resources to support that to a degree (it gets so expensive it becomes unsustainable though).

That's literally all you're doing mid-late game. Habitats for more pops to harvest more resources to fund your war campaigns. If you aren't at war, you are doing nothing but watching resource numbers go up that have no purpose except to invest to gain more resources or to spend on war.

This is really what killed the game for me. I went into it with the roleplay and culture and variety of traditions and potential playstyles and got hit with the reality that the game is only designed to devolve into war and there's literally nothing else to do.

Diplomacy is incredibly shallow which doesn't help things. The way the systems are designed it's just a strategic outpost.

Meh.

If you do buy this game, know that you will enjoy it for awhile until you get to the point where you really want to sandbox it and enjoy your species' culture and stuff only to realize it's about war. When it only is about war, why design a species around anything else but war?

I hope the devs have a lot of plans to change this up. It'd be a shame really, so much lost potential.

[i] I live in Canada and will be talking about Canadian prices and price trends. [/i]

At the time of writing, the devs have recently released a subscription model for the DLC in the game. This is not inherently a bad thing, despite what you may see in discussions. The subscription is made for new players, as stated by the dev diary #334. If you will allow me to be hyperbolic, financial barriers are made up, as this digital game could be given away for free, and it would not bankrupt paradox games. obviously that is not an effective way to continue to develop games, but the core concept is there, if the game is too expensive to play, are the devs working on ways to make it cheaper to enjoy? After a while trawling through steam databases, I can see two pieces of evidence pointing to the fact that they are not working to make the game easier to buy, and one pointing to some small efforts to help you the new player. 

The part helping new players:
Over time, the stellaris DLC's have taken longer and longer to begin to go on sale, and take even longer to reach a sale of 50%. This has changed in the last few DLC. I will use the toxoids DLC as my benchmark because that is when I feel as though the sentiment towards the DLC started to shift. The average time to go on sale for 20%, for Toxoids and the two DLC that came out before it, was 379 days. For the astral planes DLC and the two DLCs before, it took 209 days. This is a major break in the pattern of sales for stellaris. You can say I cherry picked, but I can send you my spreadsheets and graphs, this is a distinct break in the norm.
This allows players to enjoy content that may have attracted you to the game, cheaper or quicker. Additionally the game is very balanced around the presense of the DLC, and playing with all the DLC is assumed by all the stellaris media you will find. Having the recent DLC reach its maximum discount quicker allows for more people to play the primary stellaris experience.

But the two things that are hurting new players:
1. The price of the most recent DLCs are far higher than equivalent DLC that came before. The First contact story pack DLC is currently $19.99 CDN, every other story pack is $13.99 CDN. The new DLC costs more in a way completely incongruous with the entire history of the price trends of every piece of DLC in this game. There is no reason for this cost, and if it was to be more in line with long term pricing that the other DLC will catch up to when...
2. There have been three price increases for stellaris DLC in Canada in the last two years. The game costs more because of more DLC, but also every single one of those DLC has become harder to buy. The necroid DLC is the prime example of this, as it has increased from $8.99 CDN to $13.99 CDN. Necroids costs 55% more to buy right now, compared to when it was released. You can argue that they have added content to the DLC, but you could buy it at it's original price with all the new content included for a time, and even then they increased the price $1 after adding content, the other $4 had no reason to occur. The exact game and DLC I bought will cost YOU more to buy, let alone the DLC released since then.

The financial barrier of entry to this game is growing. The logical reason is that it is always gaining new DLC, and so there is more to buy, but the cost of the SAME game is increasing, and the new DLC costs more then equivalent DLC, while also having the same price increases. the price changes are far beyond inflation in Canada, there is no reason for this gouging of our wallets.

And so, Paradox created the expansion subscription. An easy solution to this[i] mysterious [/i]problem of a financial barrier that has appeared from [strike]greed[/strike] the slow growth of the library of DLC you should buy. What if you didn't own the DLC, but paid each month for a rental. Stellar idea. Case closed. See you next month.

Paradox does not care about the barrier to entry, they made it, and continue to make it today.
Paradox is hiding behind caring for new players, while bleeding their wallets dry.
YOU should not buy this game.
Find a developer that is happy to provide joy, and only asks for as much as they need to keep making the games they love.

 After 500 hours , I can confidently say I’ve almost figured out how to play. Of course, that hasn’t stopped me from making the exact same mistakes over and over again, just in more creative ways each time.
Every game starts the same... I tell myself, “This time, I’m going to be the good guy!” and I dream of a peaceful enlightened federation, where my alien neighbors and I hold hands and sing intergalactic Kumbaya. And for a while, it works. The early game feels like a wholesome Star Trek episode, all about exploration, diplomacy, and peaceful coexistence. But the game simply rewards my ego and desire too much for me not to own everything, ask yourself this: "Why have one of it, when I could have all of it?". A couple decades of boring kindness and aliens settling worlds around me go by and... oops- I've accidentally colonized my neighbors world! Its okay though, im still the good guy even though suddenly I've transformed my empire of free worlds into a surveillance-heavy police state, complete with mandatory loyalty oaths and a fleet large enough to blot out entire star systems. All it takes is a couple decades, and every game I realize the galaxy is a dangerous place, and the only path to peace is my iron fist crushing everyone else’s.

By the midgame, things take a hard turn into Star Wars territory. Alliances are shaky, fleets are massive, and some smug neighbor decides to declare war because I accidentally colonized "their" holy world. (It wasn’t holy when I found it, pal.) Cue the point in the game where I realize everything is mine, its just being warmed up for me by the xenos.

Fast forward a hundred years into the end game where I realize my computer runs better when aliens are dead. That’s when the mask of diplomacy drops, and I go full Imperium of Man on the xenos. It’s no longer about peaceful coexistence or even pragmatic alliances. No, by then, it’s about total galactic domination, fueled by centuries-old grudges against alien scum who dared to insult my empire. (Did they insult me? Maybe not. But they looked at me funny in 2304, and that’s close enough.) Suddenly, it’s me against the galaxy—a total war where even my own vassals question if they backed the wrong genocidal megalomaniac.

Jokes aside,what keeps me coming back is the infinite customization. One game, I’m a benevolent (sort of), plant-based collective spreading spores of love across the stars. The next, I’m a psychotic robot swarm assimilating everyone into my glorious machine hivemind. The sheer variety means that even after hundreds of hours, I’m still finding new ways to create, ruin, and rebuild empires.

In the grim darkness of the near future, there is only war...
